newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's Asiana gets first foreign investor.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Asiana gets first foreign investor.

text.p: South Korea's Asiana Airlines, hoping to cash in on Asia's air travel boom, on Wednesday welcomed aboard its first foreign investor after the government approved a 19.02 percent stake for Swiss Bank Corp.
Analysts applauded the linkup with the prestigious Swiss bank as a boost for Asiana, which plans to spend around $100 million annually over the next few years expanding its fleet.
"The deal will offer a strong backing to Asiana, whose parent group currently does not have financial affiliates," said Soo Sohn, analyst at ING Baring Securities in Seoul.
South Korea's Kumho Group, in which tyre maker Kumho & Co Ltd is the flagship unit, at present holds a 77.5 percent stake in the eight-year-old carrier.

The Construction and Transportation Ministry on Wednesday approved a plan by Pacific Investment Capital Ltd, a Swiss Bank unit based in Malaysia, to purchase 13.32 million out of 23.4 million new shares to be issued by Asiana.
"Our partnership with this 'triple A' bank will greatly help us raise funds more easily on overseas markets," said Suh Jae-hwan, chief of Asiana's financing department.
Asiana plans to buy 57 new planes by the year 2005 to expand its fleet to 100, Asiana's spokeswoman Michelle Han said.
Air transportation to and from South Korea has been growing rapidly and is regarded as a sector with one of the highest growth potentials in the region, analysts said.
Korean Airlines at present is the country's dominant carrier but it is increaasingly being challenged by the young Asiana.
"Korean routes are regarded as having a very high growth potential in view of the fast-growing disposable income and the economy's heavy reliance on exports," ING Baring's Sohn said.

Air passengers to and from South Korea rose by an average of 11.5 percent annually over the past five years, and the figures for calendar 1995 rose by 13.1 percent, according to the Korea Civil Aviation Development Association.
"It's one of the world's highest growth rates and the rapid pace is expected to hold on for a while," said Lee Won-shik, assistant manager at the association's statistics department.
Asiana's Han said her company carried 2.44 million passengers on international routes in 1995, up a strong 23.3 percent from 1.98 million in 1994.
But analysts said Asiana's earnings would be damaged by the won's depreciation against the dollar this year.
"We have no earnings forecasts on the company because it is not a listed firm. But its earnings will be badly affected by the won's depreciation," Sohn of ING Baring said.
The won has lost about eight percent against the dollar this year.

Asiana posted a net profit of 30.63 billion won ($36.3 million) in calendar 1995 on turnover of 1.05 trillion won, up from profits of 29.97 billion won on 794.8 billion won turnover the previous year, Asiana's Han said.
Asiana currently flies to 34 cities in 14 foreign countries and 13 cities in South Korea.
